roadmap.lecture_goal: understand how architectural design choices, from basic perceptrons to advanced neural fields, dictate the capabilities and limitations of modern deep learning models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to analyze the fundamental differences between standard neural networks and specialized architectures like SIREN, focusing on how data and architectural inductive bias constrain the hypothesis space.

You'll be able to explain the mechanics and design principles of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), including how convolution filters detect patterns, achieve translation invariance, and manage dimensionality for a.

You'll be able to evaluate advanced CNN architectures by explaining the evolution of the receptive field, the function of encoder-decoder structures (like U-Net), and the role of skip connections in enhancing deep-net'.

You'll be able to apply modern deep learning techniques to complex data types by describing the use of 3D convolutions, positional encodings, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), and contemporary video processing models.

segments.subgoal: Analyze the strengths and weaknesses of the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)

key_points.text: The Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is a universal approximator, meaning it can theoretically build any model.
MLPs are 'embarrassingly parallel,' allowing computations to be easily parallelized using hardware like GPUs.
A major drawback of MLPs is that they have weak inductive biases, making them sample inefficient and data hungry.
Dense (fully connected) layers are computationally expensive, especially when processing high-resolution image data.

key_terms.definition: Multilayer perceptron is a basic architecture where the building block consists of a linear combination of inputs, followed by a neuron-wise non-linearity, and then another linear combination.
Universal approximator is a property of a model that allows it to approximate any mathematical function.
Inductive biases are the inherent assumptions baked into a model, which dictate what structure or intuition the model assumes about the function it is trying to learn.

Dense layer, also known as a fully connected layer, is a type of layer where every neuron in the previous layer is connected to every neuron in the current layer. When processing structured data like images, this architecture requires the input to be flattened into a single long vector before computation.

segments.subgoal: Compare how data and architecture constrain the hypothesis space

key_points.text: Adding more data shrinks the space of possible models that fit the training data, potentially leading to a more optimal solution.
Defining a hypothesis space adds structure, which acts as a stronger inductive bias over the model's form.
The intersection of models that fit the data and the inductive hypothesis allows for finding better architectures even with less data.
Improving model learning can be achieved by either adding more data or by using a more constrained architecture.

key_terms.definition: Hypothesis space is a defined subset of all possible models, which adds structure to the model itself. This space shines a spotlight on a specific portion of the overall space of all possible models.
Inductive bias is a stronger prior or structure added to the model. It guides the learning process toward a specific form of model, allowing for better performance with less data.

segments.subgoal: Compare standard neural networks to SIREN to understand the role of architectural inductive bias

key_points.text: Standard models can fit training data but often generalize poorly when tested outside the training distribution.
A good neural network architecture must represent the true function while remaining minimal and easy to optimize.
SIREN uses sinusoidal activations, which introduces an inductive bias that the function distribution should be periodic.
Using SIREN allows for much more efficient convergence when fitting image data compared to models using ReLU or Tanh activations.

key_terms.definition: Architectures are structures that enable a model to generalize outside of the training distribution. A good architecture must be able to represent the true function of the data while remaining otherwise minimal.

Inductive bias is an added constraint in a model architecture that suggests a specific property about the data distribution. This bias allows the model to find solutions that adhere to that property outside of the training data.

Hypothesis space is the collection of all possible models that could potentially fit a given data point. This space is crucial because it helps the model generalize beyond the specific data it has been trained on.
Sinusoidal activation space is a model type that utilizes sinusoidal activations. This type of activation space is particularly efficient for fitting image data.

Generalization out of distribution refers to the model's ability to perform well in regions outside the data distribution, which is distinct from merely fitting the data points where training data exists.

segments.subgoal: Explain the need for local context and define semantic segmentation

key_points.text: A single label is usually insufficient to represent the semantic concepts captured in complex images because information is often locally constrained.
One initial approach to handle multiple objects is to subdivide the image into patches and classify each patch separately.
To achieve a high-resolution output, the winning idea is to use large but overlapping patches to provide local context for prediction.
The problem of categorizing every pixel instead of categorizing a whole image is called semantic segmentation.

key_terms.definition: Semantic segmentation is the problem of categorizing every pixel in an image instead of classifying the entire image as a single category. This allows the model to delineate the semantic boundaries of different objects within the image.
Patch is a small piece of the image that is subdivided and used as input for a classifier. Using patches allows the model to classify local regions of the image.

segments.subgoal: Explain how CNN architecture achieves translation invariance as an inductive bias for image categorization

key_points.text: Processing patches independently and identically makes the model invariant to translations of the input (206).
This translation invariance is considered an equivariant mapping (207).
Real-world categories possess an innate symmetry of translation invariance (217).
The model structure builds this natural symmetry into its hypothesis space (218).

key_terms.definition: Translation invariant describes a property where the classification or category of an object remains the same regardless of its location within the image. This means that an object, such as a bird, should maintain its category even if it is moved from the top corner to the center of the image.

Equivariant mapping is a type of mapping where applying a translation to the input results in a corresponding translation of the function's output. This property ensures that the model maintains a consistent relationship between input and output under spatial shifts.

Inductive bias is a hypothesis or assumption built into the model structure that guides the learning process. This bias allows the model to make sense of the data by assuming certain properties about the real world, such as translation invariance.

segments.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of convolution and how filters detect specific patterns in image data

key_points.text: Convolution is a linear, shift-invariant transformation used for filtering grid-structured input data.
The output of a convolution is calculated as a bias plus a linear combination of filter weights and pixel values, summed over the patch.
A filter produces maximum output values when the input pattern matches the filter, and minimum output when it is maximally opposite.
Filters can be designed to find specific features, such as horizontal edges between dark and light values.

key_terms.definition: Convolution is a linear, shift-invariant transformation applied to grid-structured input data. Essentially, convolution is a method used in signal processing to perform filtering.

Convolutional kernel is a set of linear weights (W) used to compute a weighted sum of pixels within a patch of data. This kernel functions as a filter, enabling a linear, shift-invariant transformation of grid-structured input data.
Filter is the set of weights used to take a linear weighted sum of the input data. This filter is designed to look for specific patterns within the input data.

segments.subgoal: Explain the structure and benefits of convolutional networks over fully connected layers

key_points.text: Convolutional networks are locally connected networks that assume the output is a local function of the input, using the same weights across the entire input (weight sharing).
The weight matrix in a convolutional layer is sparse and has a specific structure, such as a Toeplitz matrix, unlike the dense matrix of a fully connected layer.
The constraints imposed by the convolutional structure allow the network to be translation invariant and equivariant.
Because of their structure, convolutional layers can be applied to arbitrarily sized inputs without changing the learned model.

key_terms.definition: A convolutional network is essentially a locally connected network where the same weights are used regardless of where the initial input values are coming from. This structure allows the model to process local functions of the input.

A Toeplitz matrix is a specific form of matrix that arises when the weight matrix is sparse and the values are the same along the entire diagonal. This structure is characteristic of certain convolutional layers.

segments.subgoal: Explain the properties of convolutional layers and the concept of receptive field

key_points.text: Convolutional layers are translation equivariant and utilize parameter sharing for computational efficiency.
Stacking convolutional layers results in a nonlinear convolutional filter if a non-linearity is included between layers.
As more layers are added, the receptive field of the output increases.
The receptive field can be increased by making the input patch size larger or by adding more depth.

key_terms.definition: Convolutional layers are a type of layer that processes input data using filters, which allows the same parameters to be used across the entire input data. Convolutional layers are built to be equivariant to translation, meaning the output shifts if the input shifts.
Parameter sharing is a method where the same parameters are used across the entire input data. This technique allows the model to be computationally efficient by reusing weights throughout the input.
Receptive field is the area of the input image that influences a specific output unit. This field increases as more layers are added to the model's depth.
Patch processing is the ability of convolutional layers to process small, localized sections of the input data. This capability builds in explicit parallelism into the computation.

segments.subgoal: Explain how convolutional layers process multi-channel inputs and generate multi-channel outputs

key_points.text: Convolutional layers provide an inductive bias that allows for more efficient learning and better fits with less data.
Multi-channel inputs, such as RGB color, are handled by learning different weights for each input channel and summing them to get the output value.
To produce multiple output channels, a filter bank—a set of different output convolutions running in parallel—is used.
Most convolutional layers are multi-input and multi-output functions, where the number of filters determines the number of output features.

key_terms.definition: Convolutional layer is a type of layer in deep learning that performs convolutions in two dimensions, allowing it to process image data efficiently. This layer uses weights that are shared across the entire layer, which helps restrict the search space and allows for efficient learning.

Filter bank is a set of different output convolutions that are learned in parallel when a convolutional layer needs to produce multiple channels of output. Instead of learning a single linear layer, the filter bank allows the network to build multiple independent output dimensions from the same data

Multi-channel inputs refer to data that has depth, such as color images (like RGB), meaning the input is not just a spatial extent but a tensor with multiple channels. When performing convolution on these inputs, a different set of weights is learned for each input channel.

Feature channel is one of the dimensions of the output of a convolutional layer, representing a specific feature map generated by a filter. The number of feature channels corresponds to the number of filters used in the convolutional layer.

segments.subgoal: Calculate filter parameters and explain the function and complexity of convolutional layers

key_points.text: Each layer in a CNN is composed of a set of feature maps, where each map serves as a structural representation (an image) (428, 430).
The number of parameters per filter is calculated by multiplying the spatial extent dimensions (K1 x K2) by the number of input channels (C_l) (483).
The total number of filters in a bank is equal to the number of desired output channels (C_l+1) (476, 484).
Standard convolution typically refers only to the spatial extent of the filters, assuming independent weights per input channel (463, 470).

key_terms.definition: Feature map is an image that serves as a structural representation of the input data. It has height and width and is generated by applying a filter to the input.
Filter is a set of weights that is learned separately but shared across the entire image. This filter performs a linear sum over the input channels to produce a single output dimension.
Feature bank is the collection of learned output channels that a convolutional layer produces. This bank shows what different filters activate when the input image is processed.

Spatial extent refers to the dimensions of the filter, such as 3 by 3. This is the convention used when discussing filter size, focusing only on the spatial dimensions rather than the channel dimensions.
Feature collapse is a phenomenon where some features are ignored by the model. This can occur depending on the data, architecture, and optimization process.

segments.subgoal: Describe techniques for managing dimensionality and increasing context in convolutional neural networks

key_points.text: Pooling (like max pooling) reduces dimensionality and provides stability by summarizing local features.
Downsampling or strided operations are used to reduce the high-dimensional structure of the input in deep networks.
A strided operation combines convolution or pooling and downsampling by increasing the filter's stride.
A dilated filter increases the receptive field, allowing the model to gather more spatial context with fewer parameters.

key_terms.definition: Pooling is a technique applied over the output features of a convolutional layer to reduce dimensionality. Pooling uses a local window to represent the output either by taking the maximum value (max pooling) or the average value (mean pooling).

Downsampling is a method used in neural networks, particularly for classification, where the high-dimensional input structure is intentionally reduced. This is done when the network does not require the full dimensional structure at every layer.

Strided operation is a method that combines convolution or pooling with downsampling into a single element. It achieves this by increasing the stride of the filter, causing it to move further than a single pixel at each step.

Dilated filter is a type of filter where certain values are set to zero, which is baked into the model. This configuration allows the filter to capture information from a larger spatial context or extent while using fewer parameters.

segments.subgoal: Analyze the trade-offs in deep learning architecture design and training

key_points.text: Modern deep learning architectures often use small filters stacked deeply to achieve large receptive fields (573, 574, 575).
The complexity of the required network often depends on the complexity of the input image (583, 584).
Increasing the input image scale to preserve fine-grained features is often a better trade-off than excessive downsampling (587, 588).
When data is limited, incorporating inductive bias (handcrafting filters) is beneficial, but with large datasets, end-to-end learning is often preferred (605, 606).

key_terms.definition: Inductive bias refers to the constraints or prior knowledge that a model is designed with to guide its learning process. Inductive bias tends to be more beneficial when there is insufficient data, as it allows the system to optimize better by limiting the possible solutions.

Feature engineering is the historical process in computer vision and deep learning where researchers manually build handcrafted structures to help a system recognize objects. This approach involved combining these handcrafted structures into a larger system for recognition.

Receptive field describes the extent of the input that a layer processes. Large receptive fields can be generated by stacking layers deeply, allowing the network to capture a wide area despite using small initial filters.

Neural architecture search is a field of research that specifically attempts to optimize over the vast space of possible architectures. This process aims to find the best possible solution for a given task.

segments.subgoal: Explain receptive fields and how feature representations become more semantic deeper in the network

key_points.text: The receptive field determines which parts of the initial input influence a specific part of the output.
Information outside the receptive field cannot influence the model's output.
Early layers typically produce fine-grained or detailed feature activations because convolutions are highly local.
Deeper layers produce more diffuse feature activations that are semantically meaningful.

key_terms.definition: Receptive field is a concept that defines what parts of the initial input have any influence on a specific part of the output. This field dictates that the model cannot receive information from outside of this defined area.

Feature activations are the outputs of a layer that represent complex information collected from the input image. These activations can become more semantically meaningful as they pass through multiple layers of the network.

segments.subgoal: Compare encoder-decoder architectures and introduce the U-Net solution

key_points.text: Classification networks typically use filters, non-linearity, and downsampling to produce a classification output (644, 645).
Encoder-decoder architectures compress input into a low-dimensional representation and then reconstruct it using upsampling (647, 648).
The bottleneck in encoder-decoder architectures can cause the loss of fine-grained spatial structure and details (663, 665).
The U-Net architecture is designed to maintain high-resolution structure while ensuring computational efficiency (670).

key_terms.definition: Encoder-decoder architecture is a structure that processes an input by first using convolution and downsampling to create a low-dimensional representation, and then uses convolution and upsampling to reconstruct the output.
Semantic segmentation is an application of encoder-decoder architectures where the desired output space must possess spatial extent, distinguishing it from tasks that only produce a single category.
U-net is an architecture designed to bridge the gap between preserving high-resolution structure and maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for image-to-image tasks.

segments.subgoal: Explain the function and power of skip connections in deep learning architectures

key_points.text: In U-Net, skip connections allow the model to retain fine-grained spatial detail while learning semantics through an information bottleneck.
ResNet uses an identity pathway in every layer, enabling the model to implicitly learn the optimal depth for a given task.
A residual connection is fundamentally defined as the output being the function of the input plus the input dimension itself.
The ability to combine information using skip connections is a valuable computational tool also utilized in self-attention within transformers.

key_terms.definition: Skip connection is a connection across different parts of an architecture that allows information to bypass intermediate layers and pass directly toward the output. This mechanism ensures the model does not have to force fine-grained spatial detail into a low-rank embedding.
ResNet architecture is a deep learning model that utilizes a skipped connection in every single layer. This design allows the model to implicitly learn the optimal depth required for a specific task.

Residual connection is a specific type of connection where the output of a layer is calculated by adding the layer's function output to the input dimension itself. This connection assumes that the output and the residual connection are the same size.

segments.subgoal: Apply 3D convolutions to model spatio-temporal data and understand its limitations

key_points.text: Time can be treated as an additional dimension for convolutions, such as in a single scalar input over time.
Video data, combining spatial dimensions (RGB) and temporal frames, results in a four-dimensional input suitable for 3D convolutions.
3D convolutions are commonly used for tasks like action recognition in video.
A consequence of using 3D convolutions is that the model becomes shift invariant in time.

key_terms.definition: Convolutions in time involve performing convolutions over a temporal dimension, allowing the model to build representations using time as one of the dimensions.
3D convolutions are a type of convolution that operates over both spatial dimensions and a temporal dimension, resulting in a lower dimensional representation.
Shift invariant in time is a property where the model's output remains the same regardless of when an event occurs within the temporal sequence.

segments.subgoal: Explain how positional encodings and neural fields enhance convolutional architectures

key_points.text: Positional encoding adds location information to the input of convolutional filters to address the lack of shift invariance in MLPs.
A neural field is a field that is parameterized, fully or partially, by a neural network.
NeRF is a convolutional network that maps a five-dimensional coordinate grid (position and direction) to color and volumetric density.
Convolution is a fundamental operation for processing anything that has some structure, such as time or space.

key_terms.definition: Positional encoding is a method of adding location information to the input of convolutional filters. Positional encoding is constructed separately and added to the input signal, allowing the network to incorporate positional data into the convolution.

Neural field is a field that is parameterized fully or in part by a neural network. This allows the network to model a functional mapping from a coordinate grid, such as a position in an image, to an output value like color.

Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) is a popular architecture that applies a convolutional network to a map. NeRF takes a five-dimensional coordinate grid, which includes position and camera direction, as input and outputs color and volumetric density.

Convolution is a fundamental operation used for processing anything that possesses some structure, such as images or time series. Convolution involves chopping up the input into patches and applying the same function to each patch using a slide and sum operation.

segments.subgoal: Analyze the limitations and extensions of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)

key_points.text: The output of NeRF is the color of an image from a specific direction, not a complete 3D model of the scene.
NeRF is trained by taking multiple images of a scene from different positions.
Classical NeRF struggles when only a few sparse images are available or when the scene is moving.
External metadata, such as GPS location, can be incorporated into architectures by concatenation or separate convolution.

key_terms.definition: Strided convolution is a method that explicitly performs both pooling and downsampling simultaneously. This technique combines two operations into a single convolutional layer.

Pooling is a function applied to a local patch that is essentially the same as running a convolutional layer without learning weights. This function uses predefined operations, such as the maximum or average function, to constrain the layer.

segments.subgoal: Describe the computational challenges and modern architectures for video processing

key_points.text: Adding channels for all video frames (3D convolution) is computationally expensive and rarely worth it in temporal space.
State-of-the-art video models often downsample temporally because most actions can be recognized from a small number of frames.
Many advanced video models use a 'fast and slow' approach, combining low-dimensional temporal subsampling with periodic high-resolution inputs.
This two-pronged approach allows one model to model motion while the other models fine-grained semantic details.

key_terms.definition: 3D convolution is a method where channels for all different frames in a video are added, allowing the operation to slide like a window over time. This process effectively treats the video data as a volumetric input.

Fast and slow is a two-pronged approach for video processing where a low-dimensional subsampling model runs frequently to capture motion, while a secondary high-resolution channel periodically processes frames to capture fine-grained semantic details.
